findings.claim: §12.7.4 multi-maintainer configuration lists 'require_review_from_non_author: true' as a branch-protection parameter, but this is not a documented field in GitHub's legacy protected-branches REST API (/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection). The API's required_pull_request_reviews object exposes required_approving_review_count, require_code_owner_reviews, dismiss_stale_reviews, and require_last_push_approval — not require_review_from_non_author.
findings.evidence: §12.7.4 text (ADOPT-001 lines 881): 'Configure branch protection with required_approving_review_count >= 1, require_code_owner_reviews: true, and require_review_from_non_author: true.' The same term appears in plan §4 020B(viii-c): 'the caller's main branch protection must have required_approving_review_count >= 1 + dismiss_stale_reviews: true + require_review_from_non_author: true'; in 020K: 'branch-protection require_review_from_non_author=false at 020D2'; and in D-033: 'flip count=1 + codeowner=true + non-author=true'. GitHub's branch protection API for required_pull_request_reviews does not include a require_review_from_non_author field; GitHub prevents PR self-approval at the platform level implicitly regardless of this configuration. The term does not appear in configure-020f-renovate-tag-protection.sh, and enable-required-check.sh was not available for direct verification in this review pass.
findings.impact: Multi-maintainer adopters following §12.7.4 literally and constructing their branch-protection PUT payload via the API will find no require_review_from_non_author field to set. The underlying security behavior (non-self-approval) is platform-enforced regardless, so no security regression results. However, the documentation describes a configuration step that cannot be carried out as written, eroding adopter confidence and potentially causing support questions. Note: the same terminology is used consistently throughout the WP-SCP-020 plan and all prior decision records — this appears to be accepted shorthand in the plan corpus, not an error introduced by this slice — but the adopter-facing §12.7.4 is the external contract document and should use accurate API terms.
findings.mitigation: Replace 'require_review_from_non_author: true' in §12.7.4 with: 'Note: GitHub prevents PR authors from approving their own PRs at the platform level; there is no explicit API field required for this — configure required_approving_review_count >= 1 and require_code_owner_reviews: true, and GitHub enforces the non-self-approval constraint automatically.' If the term is intentionally carried over from the plan for consistency, add a parenthetical: '(require_review_from_non_author: true — platform-enforced; not a REST API field but used as shorthand in the WP-SCP-020 plan corpus)'.

findings.claim: TF-020H3-001 closure path references 'slice 020H.2' but the established WP-SCP-022 slice naming convention is '020H part N' (three existing slices: 020H part 1, 020H part 2, 020H part 3). '020H.2' is ambiguous: it parses naturally as '020H part 2', which has already merged per WP-SCP-020 §3 sequence. Neither DISPATCH-NOTE.md nor §12.7.13 explains that '020H.2' designates a new fourth slice in the sub-series.
findings.evidence: DISPATCH-NOTE.md lines 157–168: 'Closure path: open slice 020H.2 as a workflow-change PR...' ADOPT-001 §12.7.13: 'lockfile + tool-versions parity with OPA + Conftest is tracked as TF-020H3-001 → slice 020H.2'. WP-SCP-020 §3 sequence (plan lines 82–101) uses 'part N' notation throughout: '020H part 1 Cut v1.0.0-rc.1', '020H part 2 Promote v1.0.0-rc.1 → v1.0.0', '020H part 3 ADOPT-001 §12 appendix published', '020H.1 policies/VERSIONING.md + rule-RFC process + rollback detection'. The plan itself uses '020H.1' (with a period) for the post-Threshold-A slice, and '020H part N' for the pre-Threshold-A sub-slices. DISPATCH-NOTE.md TF-D1-001..003 items use 'closed in 020H part 3' (lines 74–83). No definition of '020H.2' appears in the plan, STATUS.md reference, or this DISPATCH-NOTE.
findings.impact: A contributor or automated STATUS.md parser reading 'TF-020H3-001 → 020H.2' will look for slice '020H part 2' in the STATUS.md backlog table and find it already marked closed — preventing them from correctly identifying the intended new slice and deferring closure tracking to the next session. If STATUS.md uses dotted notation (020H.1 for the post-Threshold-A slice), '020H.2' may intend a second post-Threshold-A sub-slice, but this interpretation is not stated.
findings.mitigation: In both DISPATCH-NOTE.md (lines 161, 167) and ADOPT-001 §12.7.13, replace '020H.2' with an unambiguous designator: either '020H part 4' (next in the pre-Threshold-A 'part N' series, consistent with naming of current and prior slices) or '020H.2 (a new workflow-change slice, not 020H part 2)' with an explanatory parenthetical. Align with STATUS.md's post-Threshold-A backlog naming convention when opening the slice.

findings.claim: §12.7.4 describes 'the expired-rule-config grace ramp (one-release ::warning:: window before suppression refusal at release-tag time)' as an existing v1.0.0 safety mechanism, but plan §4 020C.1(v) — the cited source — reads 'Deprecated rules emit one-release warning before removal', which refers to SCP removing a rule from its own library, not to an adopter's disable entry in rule-config reaching its expires_at date. TF-005 (which the project_020c1_tracked_forward memory attributes to the rule-config expiry grace ramp) was deferred. No expired-entry handling was found in lib/policy_check_invocation.sh lines 85–134 reviewed in this pass.
findings.evidence: ADOPT-001 §12.7.4 (line 889): 'The expired-rule-config grace ramp (one-release ::warning:: window before suppression refusal at release-tag time) is the safety-valve, not a substitute for CODEOWNERS coverage.' Plan §4 020C.1(v): 'Caller-side .scp/rule-config.yaml override with rule-level disable: <SCP-R-NNN> + justification: string + expires_at: date. Deprecated rules emit one-release warning before removal.' The 'Deprecated rules' sentence is in the context of SCP's own rule library lifecycle (a rule being deprecated by SCP), not in the context of adopter config expires_at semantics. project_020c1_tracked_forward memory: 'TF-005..TF-008 deferred to 020D2 / WP-SCP-023 / opportunistic / v1.1'. lib/policy_check_invocation.sh lines 85–134 show SCP-E002 emit paths for missing/wrong-type rule-config but no expired-entry grace-ramp logic. If expired entries are silently honored indefinitely at v1.0.0 (no suppression refusal), the described grace ramp does not exist yet and the §12.7.4 sentence misleads adopters about a present safety mechanism.
findings.impact: An adopter who lets their disable entry expire believing 'there is a one-release warning before suppression refusal' will be surprised if the workflow either (a) silently continues to disable the rule indefinitely (no warning, no refusal) or (b) immediately refuses to run without any prior warning. The mitigation guidance 'treat .scp/rule-config.yaml as a bypass-surface equivalent' and 'CODEOWNERS-protect it' is correct and valuable regardless — the misleading part is attributing an unimplemented safety valve to the grace ramp. No adopter is immediately blocked, but the documentation creates false confidence in a behavioral guarantee that may not be live.
findings.mitigation: Replace 'the expired-rule-config grace ramp (one-release ::warning:: window before suppression refusal at release-tag time) is the safety-valve' with: 'Note: a grace-ramp behavior for expired disable entries (::warning:: window before suppression refusal) is tracked as a post-v1.0.0 capability (TF-005); at v1.0.0, an expired disable entry may be silently honored or immediately refused depending on implementation state — do not rely on the grace ramp as a safety valve at this version. CODEOWNERS protection is the correct control.' Then verify TF-005 status and update once the grace ramp lands.

findings.claim: §12.7.3 states that administration:write 'also enables webhook creation, environment management, repository-transfer initiation, and archival.' Repository environment management is governed by a separate fine-grained PAT permission (environments: write) in GitHub's model, not by administration:write.
findings.evidence: §12.7.3 (ADOPT-001 line 865): 'administration:write covers more than branch-protection settings — it also enables webhook creation, environment management, repository-transfer initiation, and archival.' GitHub's fine-grained PAT repository permissions include a distinct 'Environments' permission (read / read-and-write) separate from 'Administration'. Repository webhooks are typically under 'Webhooks' as a distinct permission at the repository level, though some sources include them under Administration. Transfer and archival are standard Administration capabilities. The 'environment management' claim is the most likely inaccuracy: GitHub environments (for deployment secrets/protection rules) use the environments permission, not administration.
findings.impact: Adopters issuing a single-use administration:write PAT per §12.7.3 guidance for branch-protection configuration will not need environments access for the enable-required-check.sh operation (the script applies branch protection only). The practical risk is zero for the script's stated purpose. However, if an adopter reads this as a full inventory of what their one-time PAT grants and later uses it expecting environments access, they may be surprised when it lacks that capability. The inaccuracy slightly overstates the blast radius of the PAT, which works in the security-conservative direction.
findings.mitigation: Replace 'environment management' with a more accurate term or caveat: 'administration:write covers repository-level branch protection, some webhook operations, repository-transfer initiation, and archival — note that repository environments (deployment secrets/protection rules) require a separate environments: write permission and are NOT included in administration:write.'
